title: I feel like creating a feature or mechanic--even something small like this--should take time and iterating if you want it to be decent. How detailed do you get in your games? *Warning: A bit graphic in a low poly way*
author: Enderoth
selftext: Have any of you really done any polishing? How long did it take you to work out things like animations? It took me 4 hours just to make hands that didn't look like trash, and gripping animations came after in a tool I had to make. Vibe coding feels kinda like... I dunno,. It's really satisfying, but also not the easiest thing to get right.

comments.author: Enderoth
comments.body: Also if you have any tips, I'm all ears. Getting Claude to do things with hands can be rough. I did just figure out volumetric stuff like flames and clouds today, though, which looks like lots of fun.

comments.author: Comet7777
comments.body: Yes, any game made with AI that is considered anything above decent has spent a TON of time polishing and iteration. That isn’t the exception, it’s literally the rule in how you make good software

replies.author: PM_Me_Those_
replies.body: I think its part of the fun. Like people who literally type "make me a good game" (even if they just type a few paragraphs) are just missing the entire point of AI. Its the same reason we get total slop daily in subs like this. I fuckin love goin back and forth with AI and challenging it on ideas, but some people just think its all-knowing...

comments.author: Quirky-Map1995
comments.body: Each project get easier as u find workflows that fit your design, also there is tons of free stuff animation/assets even tho they are often not the best it can be good starting point to create ur own

comments.author: caesium23
comments.body: I mean, yeah... We're not all one-shotting prototypes. A lot of is are actually serious about making games.

comments.author: Abyssalian
comments.body:
I’ve had the same experience, I spend hours or even days editing the 'slop' out of my work. Honestly, slop isn't new.. My take is, we've seen the exact same thing for years with overused stock photos, sounds, and animations in ads and games. It's just the AI version of that now, and people will eventually get used to it. That said, yes we should put in the extra effort to make our work feel unique, and I think audiences really notice the difference.   
On the question of advice, honestly, I've read a lot of tips on reddit on specific workflows or skills and system prompts and I don't think they're very useful. Often good AI models already know what workflows work well and one will easily get into their own workflow for the specific project in question.

comments.author: Shalke97
comments.body: Should end by seeing a raised foot or fist that is rushing to the face -> Instant cut to black.
